paras: The attempted lynching of John Slater took place on the morning of 4 March 1888 in Jefferson, a suburb northwest of Chicago, when a crowd of neighbors armed with clubs, stones and a rope pursued the one-armed policeman after a wounded saloonkeeper's words were taken to accuse him of shooting. Slater, then under arrest, escaped when a police lieutenant turned his buggy and drove him to a station house. He was cleared within hours, and newspapers across the country told the story as the narrow escape of an innocent man.

Wenzel Cap kept a saloon, with a dance hall and family rooms behind it, at Wabansia Avenue and Oglesby Street in a thinly settled part of Jefferson that the Illinois Staats-Zeitung described as largely Bohemian. About 6 a.m. his 12-year-old son heard two shots and found him behind the bar, bleeding from a wound in the back of the head. Asked who had shot him, Cap said "Slater, Slater; get Slater!", naming the policeman whose beat ran past the saloon, and the boy ran out screaming that Slater had killed his father.

According to the New York Sun, an "infuriated mob" formed within an hour among neighbors who were Socialists, liked Cap and "hate the police." The Staats-Zeitung reported that men and women armed with revolvers, sticks and stones searched the neighborhood for Slater, shouting for the "bluecoat" to be hanged. Slater had gone home, where Lieutenant Switzer, officer Ulrich and Justice of the Peace Vanatte found him asleep, his revolver fully loaded.

Despite his denials, Slater was made to ride with the lieutenant to Cap's house, arriving at Oglesby and Cortland streets as a patrol wagon carried Cap away. The sight of the prisoner set off the crowd, which had procured a rope and raised cries of "Lynch him." The lieutenant wheeled the buggy a few hundred feet from the crowd and lashed the horse to the West North Avenue station, while, in the wire version, sections of the crowd cut across lots for half a mile hurling stones and sticks.

The crowd calmed after a neighboring grocer said he had seen a man resembling James Potters running bloody-faced from Cap's direction about 6 a.m. Capt. Hathaway ordered Slater released the same day but advised him not to show himself in Jefferson, and on 5 March he was back at the station. The Staats-Zeitung then reported that Cap lay in critical condition, that James Potter, alias Caruthers, was also in the hospital with a finger shattered by one of his own shots, and that he confessed.

On 6 April Jos. F. Carruthers, charged with the murder of Wenzel Cap, pleaded not guilty in the Chicago criminal court. No arrest of anyone in the crowd, and no report of Cap's death or of a trial, appears in the coverage.

The story reached readers in two wire versions and a New York Sun dispatch on 5 March. The Sun headlined it "They Wanted to Lynch Him" and blamed "Socialist" neighbors, while the wire story ran as "Bohemians Run Wild" in the Washington National Republican and the Shenandoah Herald and as "Narrow Escape of an Innocent Man" in the Indianapolis Journal. The St. Paul Daily Globe's version, "A 'Copper's' Close Call," also ran in the Yankton Press and Daily Dakotaian and the Beatrice Daily Express, and the Omaha Daily Bee and Mitchell Capital carried the wire text.

Every version stressed Slater's innocence and Cap's misunderstood words rather than the crowd's attempt itself. Only the Chicago Staats-Zeitung named the officers and followed the case into court, describing the crowd as a band of avengers and a "mordgierige Gesellschaft" (bloodthirsty company). No paper gave the race of Slater or of the crowd, which was identified by ethnicity and politics.

Accounts of the crowd differ: one wire text described several hundred Bohemian women and children, other copies added men, and the Sun and the Staats-Zeitung described men and women, the men carrying stones and revolvers. The shooter's name appears as Posters, Potter, Potters and Caruthers, and the wire's claim that Cap caught him robbing the till was reported by the Staats-Zeitung only as hearsay.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of John Slater
bases: A crowd armed with a rope pursued policeman John Slater, then in police custody, intending to lynch him for a shooting he was accused of; he escaped unhurt (A1, A2, A5).

A crowd of neighbors acting on the belief that Slater had shot saloonkeeper Wenzel Cap tried to seize and hang him without legal authority, but the officers drove him away and no one was killed (A1, A2, A5); this was an attempted lynching.

The New York Sun's correspondent (A1), two separate wire texts (A2, A3) and the Chicago Illinois Staats-Zeitung's local report (A4, A5) agree that an armed crowd tried to lynch Slater and that he escaped to the station.

accounts.label: New York Sun's Chicago dispatch
accounts.gist: A neighborhood mob of Socialists who hated the police procured a rope and set out to lynch Slater; the lieutenant wheeled his buggy a few hundred feet from the crowd and escaped to the station.

accounts.label: Wire report ('Bohemians Run Wild')
accounts.gist: Several hundred Bohemian women and children with clubs, stones and a long rope chased the officers half a mile, hurling volleys of stones and sticks, before they reached the station house.

accounts.label: Second wire report (St. Paul Globe)
accounts.gist: Slater was arrested at home and driven to the scene, where an infuriated crowd tried to lynch him before he was rapidly driven away; a man named James Potters was then identified as the shooter.

accounts.label: Illinois Staats-Zeitung local report
accounts.gist: Officers found Slater asleep with a fully loaded revolver and took him to Cap's house; the crowd rushed the buggy and one man held a rope ready, but the lieutenant turned and fled to the station; a grocer's sighting of Potters calmed the crowd.

framing.detail: The Sun headlined 'They Wanted to Lynch Him' and blamed Socialist neighbors who 'hate the police', calling them 'would-be lynchers'.
The wire story ran as 'Bohemians Run Wild' and 'Narrow Escape of an Innocent Man', stressing the ethnicity of the crowd and Slater's innocence.
The St. Paul Globe's 'A "Copper's" Close Call' told the story as a mistaken accusation and a narrow escape, without characterizing the crowd beyond 'infuriated'.
The Chicago Illinois Staats-Zeitung called the crowd a 'Racheschaar' (band of avengers) and 'mordgierige Gesellschaft' (bloodthirsty company) and stressed Slater's innocence.

info: Sunday morning, 4 March 1888; Cap was shot about 5:30-6 a.m. and the crowd pursued Slater about 8 o'clock

Jefferson, a suburb northwest of Chicago, in the Almira section northwest of Humboldt Park; Cap's saloon at the northeast corner of Wabansia Avenue and Oglesby Street; the crowd met the buggy at Oglesby and Cortland streets
John Slater, the one-armed Jefferson policeman on the beat around the saloon, known as 'one-armed Jack'; no race stated; not injured
Wounded saloonkeeper Wenzel Cap said 'Slater, get Slater', which his 12-year-old son took to mean that Slater had shot him; papers later said Cap meant only to send for the policeman

Neighbors of Cap in a Bohemian district, described by the Sun as Socialists who 'hate the police' and by the Staats-Zeitung as partly Socialists on bad terms with the police; the wire called them Bohemian women and children
